doc.title: Anat Cohen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 9, 2021

title: Tenor saxophone legacy versus the clarinet's lighter feel
summary: She says she did not choose clarinet for market reasons; the tenor's heavy legacy felt weightier than clarinet.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: In retrospect, has it been perhaps a good decision as far as finding a place in the jazz world, because there’s no lack of tenor saxophone players? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

That is correcto. There are definitely no lack of tenor saxophone players, but this, it wasn’t, as I’m saying it wasn’t like oh I want to become a clarinet player because there are plenty of tenor saxophone players. I just found myself in different situations playing clarinet and feeling really comfortable, feeling that — feeling connected to the instrument, something that maybe with a tenor saxophone was not as natural as it was for me on the clarinet. And you know the heavy, the history of jazz and the history of music, really when you think about all the spirit and the fathers of the tenor saxophone, I mean it’s such a heavy, heavy legacy, just being on the stage of the Village Vanguard and feeling like the spirit of Trane there and Joe Henderson, you know the kind of accompaniment that I had was also, you know, something that was with me the whole time. And when I play clarinet somehow, maybe because I started from more of the classical music world, I felt more connection and, oh I’m just going to play the way I play, and it wasn’t as heavy.
